::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Seperable ODE derivation](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2470609/seperable-ode-derivation), asked by [fr14](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/412287/fr14) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2017-10-13; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> Looking for some help in solving the following seperable ODE,
>
> $$\frac{d u }{d y } + 2yu = 0$$
>
> So my attempt at separating the variable gives,
>
> $$\frac{d u }{d  y \ }  = -2yu$$
>
> $$\frac{d u }{u } = -2ydy$$
>
> $$\ln u = -y^2+ c$$
>
> the final answer to this solution is $u = Ce^{-y^2}$n but I am not sure how to get this result
:::

You are nearly there.  You have
$$\ln u = -y^2 + c$$
To isolate $u$, you have to undo the ln.  The exponential function is its inverse:
$$u = e^{-y^2 + c} = e^c e^{-y^2}$$
Now let $C = e^c$.
